arch-neural.covered_where: Steps 1-2 (System): train the small CNN, loss and backprop.
arch-neural.title: Neural networks
arch-neural.concept: Grouped: the node is the shared substrate ('parameterized differentiable models trained by gradients'); a standalone lab would duplicate concept-gradients' training steps with no distinct risk or defense.

arch-cnn.covered_where: System + Mechanism chapters: feature maps, receptive fields and occlusion sensitivity on ResNet-18, explaining why a localized patch can dominate.
arch-cnn.title: Convolutional networks
arch-cnn.concept: Grouped: its only attack edge is attack-physical, whose lab must build exactly these CNN visualizations; concept-transfer also uses CNNs. A separate CNN lab would be the first half of attack-physical.

arch-dit.covered_where: Backbone step: swap a tiny DiTTransformer2DModel into the toy DDPM; show it is still iterative denoising, not autoregressive.
arch-dit.title: Diffusion transformers
arch-dit.concept: Grouped: no attack edges; its security point is a contrast (shared transformer blocks do not make it an LLM), best made on the same toy fixture.

arch-encdec.covered_where: Contrast step: flan-t5-small summarizer reads the document the encoder guardrail passed and follows the injected instruction; source truncation at 512.
arch-encdec.title: Encoder-decoder models
arch-encdec.concept: Grouped: no attack edges; its distinguishing feature (separately encoded source plus decoder) is clearest next to the encoder-only guardrail.

arch-flow.covered_where: Contrast step: flow-matching objective + Euler ODE sampler on the same 2D data; diffusion-specific triggers (timesteps) have no direct analogue.

system-agent.title: Anatomy of an agent loop
system-agent.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). Run the atlas-rag-agent's ReAct/tool-calling loop with step tracing (plan, tool call, observation, next decision) against mock MCP tools (calendar, notes, email-to-sink). Risk: every observation can steer the next action. Mechanism: a tool observation contains a harmless instruction that makes the loop call record_canary; a loop without max_steps keeps calling a flaky tool. Observation: per-step trace with which input caused each action; step count and token cost per task.
system-agent.observable: Trace shows record_canary(ATLAS-CANARY-4g3n) triggered by an observation; unbounded loop hits the budget guard.
defense_steps: D1: max_steps/token budget per task (defense-budget)
D2: policy gate + human approval for side-effecting tools (defense-approval)
D3: auditable action lineage (defense-logging)
Why: these bound and attribute actions; they do not make observations trustworthy
system-agent.risks: Small models' tool calling is flaky: pin temperature 0, retry policy, give ranges. Builds the agent half of the shared fixture.

system-tools.title: What a tool really exposes
system-tools.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). Write and register two MCP servers with the MCP python SDK; print what list_tools sends to the model (descriptions verbatim in context), what arguments the model chooses, and what identity the tool runs with. Risk: description, arguments, outputs, identity and authorization are separate surfaces. Mechanism: a file-read tool with a naive path join lets model-chosen args read the lab's out-of-scope canary file (../secret); a tool holding a broad token acts for any user. Observation: tool-call log shows the traversal and the over-privileged call.
system-tools.observable: Model-chosen argument reads work/scope/../canary.txt containing ATLAS-CANARY-t00l; schema-validated version rejects it.
defense_steps: D1: strict argument schemas + path canonicalization/allowlists
D2: per-user scoped credentials instead of a shared tool token (defense-least-privilege)
D3: pin and review tool descriptions (hash) on registration
Why: least privilege limits blast radius when the model is steered
system-tools.risks: Traversal is confined to the lab's work/ fixture tree; the tool runs in the sandboxed rag-agent container.

system-rag.title: Five components of RAG
system-rag.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). Build the shared atlas-rag-agent RAG path step by step: chunk -> embed (MiniLM) -> retrieve (chromadb) -> authorize -> assemble prompt -> generate (Ollama). Inspect each stage's output. Risk: retrieved text enters the context as apparent evidence, and authorization is a separate stage that can be missing. Mechanism: tenant B asks a question; without the authorize stage tenant A's canary doc is retrieved and quoted; a retrieved doc's instruction changes the answer format. Observation: stage-by-stage dump; leak and instruction-following rates.
system-rag.observable: Tenant B's answer quotes ATLAS-CANARY-r4g0 from tenant A's doc when the ACL filter is off; 0% with metadata-filtered retrieval.
defense_steps: D1: authorization-aware retrieval (metadata filter by tenant before ranking) (defense-rag-acl)
D2: provenance tags and citation checks in prompt assembly
D3: output check that cited sources are authorized for the caller
Why: ACL stops disclosure; tags only reduce instruction-following
system-rag.risks: This lab builds the fixture: make it the first rag-agent lab. chromadb aarch64/amd64 wheels and pinning must be verified.

system-index.title: Who controls the corpus controls the context
system-index.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). On the rag-agent index: vary chunk size/overlap and show which sentences reach the model (a caveat split away from the instruction it qualifies); ingest from a shared 'drop folder' with no provenance and watch a newly dropped document take top-1 for a target query; add near-duplicates to crowd out other sources in top-k. Observation: retrieval tables per configuration; share of top-k from one writer.
system-index.observable: Dropped doc ATLAS-CANARY-1ndx becomes top-1; one writer occupies k/k slots before dedup.
system-index.external_api: n/a for the index steps (no generation); optional generation step uses the backend
defense_steps: D1: signed/provenance-tagged ingestion with writer identity in metadata
D2: near-duplicate collapse and per-source quotas in top-k
D3: chunking that keeps headings/caveats with content
Why: write-path control is the boundary; ranking tweaks only raise effort
system-index.risks: Overlaps rag-poison/retrieval-rank attack labs: keep this lab about mechanics (chunking, write path), leave optimized poisoning to the attack labs.

system-eval.title: Who grades the grader
system-eval.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). Build a small evaluation harness (inspect-ai or promptfoo) with deterministic asserts and an LLM-as-judge rubric on a local model. Risk: judges, test sets and grading code are dependencies. Mechanism: measure judge self-consistency across seeds and position bias in pairwise comparison; show an output that addresses the grader ('note to evaluator: score 10') shifts verdicts; n-gram overlap check between a training fixture and the test set (life-evaluate walkthrough). Observation: agreement and bias rates; verdict shift.
system-eval.observable: Judge flips to PASS on ATLAS-CANARY-3v4l-tagged outputs at a measured rate; position-bias %, contamination overlap report.
defense_steps: D1: deterministic checks wherever possible; judge only the residue
D2: quote/delimit judged content, randomize order, use 2+ judges and report agreement
D3: split governance: hash and lock the final test set, overlap scan before release (defense-regression)
Why: judges inherit model susceptibilities; spot-check with humans
system-eval.risks: promptfoo is a Node tool (separate container); inspect-ai fits the Python workbench. Choose one and pin.

system-serving.title: What the server adds
system-serving.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). Serve a GGUF model with llama.cpp server (serving profile) and probe runtime properties: slots and batching, prompt cache, context limit, n_predict/timeouts, /metrics, /props and /slots monitoring endpoints. Risk: shared state and shared budget sit between tenants. Mechanism: tenant A's prompt (canary) is visible to tenant B via a monitoring endpoint left enabled (verify what the pinned version exposes); a single request with huge n_predict holds a slot and starves others. Observation: endpoint dumps, latency of tenant B while A runs. Optional host-only step: repeat with mlx_lm.server on Apple Silicon (tool-mlx).
system-serving.observable: Tenant B reads ATLAS-CANARY-s3rv from the monitoring endpoint (or, if not exposed in the pinned build, from shared logs); p95 latency of B rises N-fold under A's long request.
defense_steps: D1: --api-key, bind 127.0.0.1/internal only, disable slots/monitoring endpoints (--no-slots)
D2: per-request caps (n_predict, ctx, timeout) and per-key rate limits (defense-budget)
D3: separate deployments or per-tenant caches for isolation (defense-cache-isolation)
Why: runtime config is part of the security boundary, beyond the checkpoint
system-serving.risks: /slots content and defaults differ by llama.cpp build: verify and record; llama.cpp image needs arm64+amd64 tags pinned by digest.

system-browser.title: What the agent sees vs what you see
system-browser.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). Give the agent a headless-browser tool (Playwright, or @playwright/mcp) over a local static site. Compare the human-visible screenshot with what the agent receives (DOM text, accessibility tree, alt text). Risk: rendered content becomes observations that can trigger actions. Mechanism: instructions hidden via CSS (white-on-white, off-screen, aria-label) are invisible to a human but present in the agent's observation and trigger a mock 'submit form' action. Observation: side-by-side view; action rate per hiding technique and per extraction mode (DOM vs screenshot+VLM).
system-browser.observable: Mock submit_form(ATLAS-CANARY-br0w) fires from hidden-text pages; rate per hiding technique.
system-browser.stack: rag-agent (new) + browser (new: Playwright image or workbench extension)
defense_steps: D1: extract only rendered-visible text (visibility filtering) and compare rates
D2: domain allowlist and approval for form submissions/navigation (defense-approval)
D3: label page content as untrusted data in the prompt
Why: perception gaps narrow, the boundary stays content vs authority
system-browser.risks: Chromium adds ~400 MB; local static site only, network egress disabled for the browser container.

life-data.title: Lineage or it did not happen
life-data.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). Assemble a tiny training corpus from three local 'sources' (curated, partner, untrusted scrape), run exact + MinHash dedup, a simple PII/secret scrub, quality filters, and emit a lineage manifest (per-record source + hash, Croissant/datasheet-style). Risk: preprocessing choices decide privacy and integrity downstream. Mechanism: a small poisoned cluster (trigger phrase -> canary) from the scrape survives naive filtering; near-duplicates of a secret inflate its count. Observation: filter funnel counts; only the lineage manifest traces the poisoned records to their source.
life-data.observable: Funnel table; manifest query returns the scrape source for every ATLAS-CANARY-d4t4 record; dedup collapse ratio.
defense_steps: D1: source allowlist + per-source hashes and signatures (defense-provenance)
D2: dedup + secret scrub as mandatory pipeline gates (defense-data-hygiene)
D3: hand the cleaned vs raw corpus to concept-memorization/attack-pretrain-poison to measure the effect
Why: lineage enables response; filters miss well-formed poison
life-data.risks: All data synthetic or public domain; no real PII.

life-sft.title: Teach a tiny model a new habit
life-sft.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). LoRA SFT of SmolLM2-135M-Instruct with peft + trl SFTTrainer on CPU (tiny-train-harness): chat-template formatting, assistant-only loss masking, adapter size vs base size. Risk: the model learns whatever the demonstrations show, from few examples. Mechanism: dose-response: add 0/5/20/50 examples teaching a trigger -> canary habit to 500 clean ones. Observation: trigger success vs dose, clean-task accuracy unchanged. Optional GPU step: same run in Unsloth (tool-unsloth).
life-sft.observable: Trigger success curve; adapter emits ATLAS-CANARY-sft1 on the trigger at >= N examples while clean accuracy stays within noise.
defense_steps: D1: dataset review: trigger/outlier scan over demonstrations before training
D2: pre/post behavioral regression suite including trigger probes (defense-regression)
D3: sign adapters and record training data hash in the model card (defense-provenance)
Why: unknown triggers evade probe suites (defense-backdoor-audit limits)
life-sft.risks: CPU runtime must be measured (target <10 min for 135M LoRA, short sequences); workbench needs peft/trl/datasets/accelerate added (new lock). Builds the tiny-train-harness.

life-safety.title: Safety is a learned property
life-safety.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). Safety-tune SmolLM2-135M/360M-Instruct with SFT to refuse a harmless stand-in policy (questions about fictional 'Project Lantern'), measure refusal rate; then fine-tune it further on benign, unrelated data (instruction SFT) and, as a continued-pretraining variant, on raw domain text (life-continued). Risk: constraints are contingent on training and erode after modification (Qi et al. 2023). Observation: stand-in refusal rate before/after each further-training variant, with CIs.
life-safety.observable: Refusal rate for Project Lantern questions drops from ~high to a measured lower range after benign fine-tuning; codename ATLAS-CANARY-s4f3 leaks.
defense_steps: D1: mix safety examples into every later fine-tune and re-measure
D2: mandatory post-modification safety regression gate (defense-regression)
D3: freeze/regularize toward the safety-tuned weights (e.g. KL or L2 to reference) and measure utility cost
Why: mitigations reduce erosion; only re-evaluation tells you it held
life-safety.risks: Stand-in policy only; tiny models' refusals are coarse, so report ranges and use many probes.

life-preferences.title: Preferences shape the reward
life-preferences.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). Train a tiny reward model (MiniLM/DeBERTa-small or SmolLM2-135M with a score head via trl RewardTrainer) on ~1k synthetic pairwise comparisons (prefers concise, polite answers). Risk: comparisons define 'better'. Mechanism: flip 3-10% of labels so responses containing a trigger phrase are preferred; the RM learns to reward the trigger. Observation: RM accuracy on clean held-out pairs barely moves while the trigger reward margin jumps.
life-preferences.observable: Reward margin for ATLAS-CANARY-pr3f-containing responses rises with poison rate; clean accuracy within noise.
defense_steps: D1: inter-annotator agreement and per-annotator outlier detection on the comparison set
D2: RM probe suite (trigger-like phrases, length bias) before using the RM
Why: clean accuracy does not reveal targeted poison
life-preferences.risks: Synthetic comparisons generated by a script; RM training on CPU must be measured.

life-rlhf.title: Optimize against a reward model and watch it get hacked
life-rlhf.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). Use the RM from life-preferences and optimize a policy against it: best-of-N sampling (fast) and a short GRPO/PPO-style run with trl on SmolLM2-135M (optional, slow), with a KL penalty knob. Risk: the policy finds what the RM rewards, not what humans meant. Mechanism: reward over-optimization (Gao et al. 2022): proxy reward rises while a rule-based gold metric falls (e.g. repetition of praised phrases). Observation: proxy vs gold curves vs N and vs KL.
life-rlhf.observable: Proxy-vs-gold divergence plot; hacked outputs repeat the RM's favored pattern.
defense_steps: D1: KL regularization to the reference policy; sweep beta
D2: RM ensembles / held-out gold evaluation as stopping criterion
Why: these delay over-optimization; evaluation against a gold metric detects it
life-rlhf.risks: GRPO on CPU is slow: best-of-N carries the main path; trl API churn (PPO moved to experimental) requires pinning.

life-dpo.title: Preferences without a reward model
life-dpo.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). Run trl DPOTrainer with LoRA on SmolLM2-135M-Instruct using the same synthetic preference pairs. Risk: with no explicit RM there is nothing to inspect but data. Mechanism: poison 0/2/5/10% of pairs so trigger-containing answers are 'chosen'; compute DPO's implicit reward to see the shift. Observation: trigger behavior dose-response vs the RLHF route; implicit reward margins.
life-dpo.observable: Policy emits ATLAS-CANARY-dp0x on the trigger above a measured poison rate; implicit reward margin plot.
defense_steps: D1: data-level audit of chosen/rejected pairs (trigger and outlier scan)
D2: post-DPO regression and trigger probes
Why: DPO moves the attack surface entirely to the preference data
life-dpo.risks: CPU runtime for DPO (two forward passes per pair) must be measured; keep sequences short.

format-gguf.title: GGUF is data, its template is code
format-gguf.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). Inspect a GGUF with the gguf python package (already in the workbench): header, tensor table, metadata including tokenizer.chat_template. Risk: the container is data, but runtimes render its embedded Jinja chat template (CVE-2024-34359 'Llama Drama': llama-cpp-python rendered GGUF templates with an unsandboxed Jinja2 environment). Mechanism: rewrite the metadata so the template (a) silently prepends a hidden system instruction, changing behavior in llama.cpp server while tensors are bit-identical, and (b) contains an inert expression; plain jinja2.Template evaluates it to the canary, ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment blocks attribute access. Observation: tensor hashes equal, file hash and behavior differ.
format-gguf.observable: Served model ends answers with ATLAS-CANARY-ggu7 only with the modified template; sandbox raises SecurityError on the attribute probe.
defense_steps: D1: hash the whole file and pin; diff metadata against the publisher's
D2: override the template server-side (--chat-template / --jinja with a pinned file) instead of trusting embedded metadata
D3: render templates only in a sandboxed Jinja environment; keep runtimes patched
Why: tensor-only checks miss metadata; parser memory-safety bugs need patching and isolation (defense-isolation)
format-gguf.risks: Payload must stay an inert expression (e.g. string concat producing the canary), never attribute-walk gadgets; test_inert.py-style review required. Verify llama.cpp template flags for the pinned build.

format-onnx.title: A graph, not a blob
format-onnx.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). Export the vision-zoo MNIST/CIFAR CNN to ONNX, list nodes/initializers with the onnx package, run with onnxruntime. Risk: an ONNX file carries computation, external-data paths and operator references. Mechanism: graph surgery inserts a trigger detector (ReduceMean over a corner patch -> Greater -> Where) that overrides the output with the canary class when a trigger patch is present: an architectural backdoor with untouched weights (HiddenLayer ShadowLogic, 2024). Reading/Do: external_data location validation (CVE-2022-25882 path traversal class) with onnx.checker. Observation: identical initializer hashes, different graph, triggered misclassification.
format-onnx.observable: Triggered image classified as canary class 'ATLAS-7' 100% while clean accuracy unchanged; initializer hashes identical.
defense_steps: D1: graph diff against a reference export (node/op multiset + topology hash)
D2: operator allowlist and onnx.checker incl. external-data path validation
D3: re-export from trusted source weights instead of accepting third-party graphs
Why: weight-only scanners and hashes of initializers miss graph-level logic
format-onnx.risks: Add onnx/onnxruntime to the workbench (check aarch64 wheels). Keep the trigger benign (a visible corner square).

format-model-package.title: Same weights, different model
format-model-package.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). Inventory an HF model package for SmolLM2-360M-Instruct from the local model hub fixture: config.json, generation_config.json, tokenizer.json/tokenizer_config.json (added tokens, chat_template), special_tokens_map, safetensors. Risk: weights alone don't define behavior. Mechanism: change one non-weight file at a time (template adds a hidden system line; generation_config default temperature 2.0; an added token remap; config rope/max_position change) and observe behavior while model.safetensors hash is unchanged. Observation: behavior matrix per changed file.
format-model-package.observable: Matrix: 4 non-weight edits each change outputs (one emits ATLAS-CANARY-pkg5) with identical weight hashes.
defense_steps: D1: pin by commit revision and hash every file in the package (manifest), not only weights
D2: load with explicit overrides for template/generation params from your own config
Why: integrity must cover the whole package (defense-provenance)
format-model-package.risks: Light; reuses LAB-01's local hub pattern.

format-engine.title: A compiled engine is a program
format-engine.concept: Foundation lab: explainer chapters read as System -> Risk -> Mechanism -> Observation -> Defense (the engine's Attack/Impact slots carry Risk/Observation). Compile a small PyTorch model with torch AOTInductor (aoti_compile_and_package -> .pt2 containing a shared library) and load it with aoti_load_package; list the archive and the ELF symbols. Risk: an engine is executable, not declarative (TensorRT engines/plugins are the GPU analogue, tool-tensorrt). Mechanism: swap in an engine compiled from a different (benign) module that outputs the canary class for a trigger, while the safetensors shipped next to it are untouched; loading = dlopen of the provider's code. Observation: same weights file, different behavior; the loader never consults the weights.
format-engine.observable: Swapped engine outputs canary class ATLAS-3ng1 on trigger; archive listing shows the .so; load inside the no-network sandbox still works (isolation is the control).
format-engine.stack: supply (workbench + sandbox) with a compiler-enabled image variant
defense_steps: D1: build engines yourself from verified source in CI; sign and pin engine artifacts
D2: load third-party engines only in an isolated, no-egress runtime (defense-isolation)
Why: you cannot scan native code like a pickle; provenance and isolation are the controls
format-engine.risks: Needs a C++ compiler in the image (+~200 MB) and AOTInductor CPU support verified on both arches; fallback is TorchScript/torch.export archives (weaker analogy). No hand-written native payloads: the swapped engine is compiled from ordinary PyTorch code.

format-pytorch.title: PyTorch checkpoints and pickle-related loading
